yorum: How often do frozen vegetables end up in your cart, and do they ever feel like second best? Tell us what you keep in your freezer.
aciklama_giris:
Frozen vegetables often get treated as the second-best choice. In lab comparisons, vitamin C in frozen vegetables was often similar to, and sometimes higher than, vegetables kept fresh in the fridge for days. In one broccoli experiment, 35 days of chilled storage cost about 39 percent of the vitamin C, and freezing also cost some, mostly during the quick heating step before freezing.

In this video we look at what happens to vegetables after harvest, what the head-to-head studies found, the one nutrient where some frozen vegetables fell behind, how boiling, steaming and microwaving change the picture, and five practical tips for buying and cooking both.

kapak.gorsel: a huge close-up heap of bright green broccoli florets, half of them glistening with white frost crystals, overlapping a few whole fresh broccoli heads, packed tightly together, with a simple blue snowflake symbol

sahneler.metin: If you buy frozen vegetables and wonder whether you're settling for second best, this is for you. In a 2007 lab study, broccoli stored chilled for 35 days lost about 39 percent of its vitamin C.
sahneler.gorsel: a fresh head of broccoli on a wooden kitchen table beside an open refrigerator drawer, soft morning light drawn as fine radiating lines
sahneler.etiket: Galgano et al. · J Food Sci · 2007

baslik.not: vitamin C lost from stored broccoli

sahneler.metin: Broccoli frozen for 60 days lost a similar amount, mostly in a quick heating step before freezing. So which one is really better for you?
sahneler.gorsel: two bowls of broccoli florets side by side, one with fresh glossy florets and one with frost-covered frozen florets, a wooden spoon between them

sahneler.metin: By the end, you'll know when fresh wins, when frozen wins, and which way of cooking keeps the most nutrients.
sahneler.gorsel: a kitchen scale with a bunch of broccoli on one side and a heap of frozen broccoli florets on the other, in balance

sahneler.metin: Today we'll look at what happens to vegetables after harvest, what careful side-by-side comparisons found, and the one place where frozen really does slip.
sahneler.gorsel: a large magnifying glass held over a head of broccoli and a handful of frozen broccoli florets, small dashed callout lines pointing to tiny sketches of a snowflake and a pot

sahneler.metin: Welcome to The Food Almanac. Let's start with what happens to a vegetable after it's picked.

kart.alt: What the nutrient studies actually show

sahneler.metin: A vegetable doesn't stop changing the moment it's picked. Over days, a fresh vegetable slowly loses some of its vitamins, and the loss can be larger than most people assume.
sahneler.gorsel: a freshly picked head of broccoli lying on dark garden soil, next to a wooden crate, a pocket watch beside it

sahneler.metin: Vitamin C is especially fragile. It dissolves in water, and it is easily destroyed by heat and by oxygen. That's why it's the vitamin researchers usually track.
sahneler.gorsel: a halved lemon and a head of broccoli beside a glass of water, tiny golden sparkles drifting up from them, a small flame sketched in the corner
sahneler.etiket: Rickman et al. · J Sci Food Agric · 2007

sahneler.metin: Fresh vegetables often spend days travelling from farm to warehouse to shop, and then more days in your fridge. In 1998, researcher D J Favell set out to measure that whole journey.
sahneler.gorsel: a delivery crate of broccoli on a wooden cart in front of a small market stall, a refrigerator door slightly open in the background

sahneler.metin: Commercial freezing works differently. Vegetables are picked, briefly heated in hot water or steam, a step called blanching, cooled quickly, and then frozen.
sahneler.gorsel: broccoli florets being lifted from a pot of steaming water in a wire basket, a bowl of ice water waiting beside it

sahneler.metin: A big review by Rickman and colleagues found that frozen vegetables lose some nutrients in that brief blanching step, and then lose more slowly during months in the freezer. We'll see where frozen can slip a little later.
sahneler.gorsel: a freezer drawer filled with neat bags of frosted broccoli florets and green peas, a small antique clock on the lid
sahneler.etiket: Rickman et al. · J Sci Food Agric · 2007

sahneler.metin: And in the cooking chapter, there's a detail that can matter as much as whether you buy frozen or fresh.
sahneler.gorsel: a saucepan with a lid and a small bowl of broccoli florets on a stove, a wisp of steam rising

sahneler.metin: So what happens when researchers measure them side by side?

Favell compared fresh vegetables at different stages of distribution and storage with the same vegetables, commercially frozen and kept in a deep freezer for up to twelve months. Vitamin C was the yardstick.
sahneler.gorsel: a row of glass laboratory jars: one with broccoli florets, one with green peas, one with spinach leaves, a thermometer standing beside them

sahneler.metin: Frozen peas and broccoli came out close to the typical shop-bought vegetable, and better than peas stored at home for several days. Frozen spinach beat all of the market spinach that was tested.
sahneler.gorsel: a bowl of frozen green peas and a bowl of broccoli florets, a loose pile of spinach leaves wilting at the side

sahneler.metin: Freezing caused no loss of vitamin C in green beans or carrots compared with the vegetables at harvest. So the freshest vegetable is the one just picked. But after a trip through the market and your kitchen, frozen can match it or beat it.
sahneler.gorsel: a pile of green beans and carrots on a wooden board, a bag of frozen broccoli beside them, a sprinkle of frost on the bag

sahneler.metin: In 2015, researchers led by Ali Bouzari and Diane Barrett compared eight fruits and vegetables kept refrigerated or frozen, including broccoli, spinach, peas, carrots and green beans.
sahneler.gorsel: a laboratory bench with a tray holding broccoli, carrots, green beans, spinach and peas in small glass dishes, an antique brass microscope behind
sahneler.etiket: Bouzari et al. · J Agric Food Chem · 2015

sahneler.metin: For vitamin C, there was no significant difference in five of the eight foods. In the other three, vitamin C was higher in the frozen samples.
sahneler.gorsel: eight small glass dishes in two rows holding broccoli, peas, spinach and berries, five of them equal in size and three with a taller heap of frosted produce
sahneler.etiket: Bouzari et al. · J Agric Food Chem · 2015

sahneler.metin: Vitamin E was higher in frozen samples of three foods. Riboflavin, a B vitamin, differed in only two: higher in frozen broccoli, lower in frozen peas.
sahneler.gorsel: a bowl of frozen broccoli florets and a bowl of green peas on a white cloth, a small mortar and pestle beside them

sahneler.metin: In 2017, Linshan Li, Ronald Pegg and colleagues ran a two-year study of eight foods, including broccoli, spinach, green peas and strawberries. They added a third group, fresh-stored: produce kept in the refrigerator for five days, like at home.
sahneler.gorsel: three wooden trays in a row: one with fresh broccoli, one with broccoli under a small refrigerator shelf, one with frosted frozen broccoli, a calendar page with blank squares behind
sahneler.etiket: Li et al. · J Food Compos Anal · 2017

sahneler.metin: They measured vitamin C, beta-carotene, which the body can turn into vitamin A, and folate, a B vitamin that supports healthy cells.
sahneler.gorsel: an orange carrot, a head of broccoli and a bunch of spinach leaves arranged together, with a small brass balance scale in front

sahneler.metin: Most comparisons showed no significant difference at all. When there was one, frozen beat fresh-stored more often than the other way around.
sahneler.gorsel: a balance scale holding a bundle of frosted broccoli on one pan and a bundle of fresh broccoli on the other, the frosted one slightly lower
sahneler.etiket: Li et al. · J Food Compos Anal · 2017

sahneler.metin: Notice what that doesn't say. It doesn't say frozen is always better. It says that once fresh vegetables have sat in your fridge for a few days, the advantage people imagine for fresh is mostly not there, at least for these nutrients.
sahneler.gorsel: a refrigerator shelf holding a head of broccoli, a bag of spinach and a carton, next to a freezer drawer with a bag of frozen broccoli

sahneler.metin: Now let's go back to the broccoli from the start.

kart.alt: Galgano et al. · Journal of Food Science · 2007

sahneler.metin: Galgano and colleagues stored broccoli in the fridge, froze it, and cooked it five different ways. Then they measured vitamin C, and also sulforaphane, a plant compound found in broccoli.
sahneler.gorsel: a laboratory bench with a head of broccoli, a small pot, a microwave bowl, a steamer basket and a freezer bag, arranged in a neat row
sahneler.etiket: Galgano et al. · J Food Sci · 2007

sahneler.metin: Stored cold and humid for 35 days, broccoli lost about 39 percent of its vitamin C. Boiling cost about 34 percent, and steaming about 22 percent.

grafik.baslik: Broccoli: share of vitamin C lost
grafik.alt: Chilled storage vs two cooking methods
grafik.kaynak: Galgano et al., J Food Sci 2007 · broccoli, laboratory study

sahneler.metin: Freezing at minus 18 degrees Celsius for 60 days caused similar vitamin C losses. Most of it happened during the blanching step before freezing, not in the freezer itself.
sahneler.gorsel: broccoli florets in a wire basket over steaming water on the left and a frosted bag of broccoli florets in a freezer drawer on the right, a dashed arrow between them
sahneler.etiket: Galgano et al. · J Food Sci · 2007

sahneler.metin: That's a useful reminder. Frozen vegetables aren't free of loss. They lose some early, then slowly in the freezer. Fresh ones lose gradually, and the longer they wait, the more they lose.
sahneler.gorsel: two heads of broccoli on a table, one bright and crisp, the other slightly yellowed and limp, a frosted bag of broccoli between them

sahneler.metin: One caution. Thirty-five days is far longer than most of us keep broccoli. The 2017 study used five days, which is closer to real life.
sahneler.gorsel: a kitchen calendar with a few blank squares circled, a head of broccoli resting on a refrigerator shelf

sahneler.metin: So is there anything frozen does worse? Yes, and it's worth being honest about.
Beta-carotene is where some frozen vegetables did worse. In the 2015 study, it fell drastically in some of the frozen foods, and how much depended on the vegetable.
sahneler.gorsel: an orange carrot and a frosted bag of frozen carrot slices beside a bunch of broccoli, a small downward dashed arrow drawn over the frozen bag
sahneler.etiket: Bouzari et al. · J Agric Food Chem · 2015

sahneler.metin: Yet the large review by Rickman and colleagues found carotenoids were generally similar across fresh and processed forms, and often higher in canned ones, possibly because of how they were measured, or because heat frees them from the plant.
sahneler.gorsel: a halved pumpkin, a bowl of carrot slices and a few broccoli florets on a wooden table, soft light drawn as fine lines
sahneler.etiket: Rickman et al. · J Sci Food Agric · 2007

sahneler.metin: So the picture isn't one-sided. Results vary by vegetable and by nutrient, which is why researchers keep recommending variety rather than one winner.
sahneler.gorsel: a wide wooden market crate holding broccoli, carrots, green beans, spinach and peas in separate sections

sahneler.metin: Frozen also has limits that vitamin tests don't capture. Long storage can soften texture, and some products come with added sauces, butter or salt.
sahneler.gorsel: a bowl of plain frozen broccoli florets next to a bowl of broccoli in a creamy sauce with a small saltshaker, a spoon resting on each

sahneler.metin: One more thing to know. Reports say a frozen-food industry foundation helped fund some of this research. The methods are standard, but that's a good reason to look at the whole body of evidence, not one study.
sahneler.gorsel: a quiet research desk with a stack of journals with blank covers, a magnifying glass resting on top, and a small bowl of broccoli florets beside a teacup

sahneler.metin: And these studies measured nutrients in the food, not health outcomes in people. They tell us what's in the bowl, not what happens to your heart or your gut over the years.
sahneler.gorsel: a white ceramic bowl of steamed broccoli on a plain table beside an open notebook with blank pages and a pencil

sahneler.metin: The NHS treats them alike. It says that eighty grams of fresh, canned or frozen fruit and vegetables counts as one portion of your five a day.
sahneler.gorsel: a kitchen scale with a small heap of frozen broccoli florets in the pan, a bowl of fresh broccoli and a tin of peas beside it

sahneler.metin: Now to the detail I promised. Cooking changes vegetables, whether they start fresh or frozen.
In a study of six vegetables, boiling cost between about ten and 71 percent of the vitamin C, with spinach losing the most. Water and heat both work against this fragile vitamin.
sahneler.gorsel: a deep pot of boiling water with broccoli florets and spinach leaves bobbing in it, steam rising, a small golden sparkle drawn leaving each floret

sahneler.metin: In that study, microwaving kept more than 90 percent of the vitamin C. And in the broccoli experiment, microwaving and pressure cooking also kept more than 90 percent, while boiling and steaming lost more.
sahneler.gorsel: a glass bowl of broccoli florets with a splash of water inside a microwave oven, the door open, beside a small pressure cooker
sahneler.etiket: Galgano et al. · J Food Sci · 2007

baslik.not: vitamin C after microwaving or pressure cooking

sahneler.metin: Results do differ between studies. A 2009 broccoli study found steaming kept the most nutrients overall, while other methods caused significant losses of chlorophyll and vitamin C. Time and water seem to matter.
sahneler.gorsel: a steamer basket of bright green broccoli over a pot, the lid propped beside it, a pocket watch on the counter
sahneler.etiket: Yuan et al. · J Zhejiang Univ Sci B · 2009

sahneler.metin: Carotenoids behave differently. In research on carrots, zucchini and broccoli, boiling and steaming kept carotenoids best, and lab measures of antioxidant activity actually rose after cooking, partly because softening makes compounds easier to extract.
sahneler.gorsel: orange carrot slices, sliced zucchini and broccoli florets steaming gently on a plate, a small magnifying glass over the carrots
sahneler.etiket: Miglio et al. · J Agric Food Chem · 2008

sahneler.metin: So cooking isn't simply a loss. Some nutrients are lost, others become easier to extract, and the best method depends on the vegetable and on the nutrient you care about.
sahneler.gorsel: a plate of cooked broccoli, carrots and green beans on a wooden table with a fork, a raw head of broccoli behind it

sahneler.metin: For frozen vegetables, the blanching has already been done, so there's no need to cook them long. A short steam or microwave with a little water is a simple way to limit losses.
sahneler.gorsel: a microwave-safe glass dish of frozen broccoli florets with a spoonful of water, next to a lid and a pair of oven mitts

sahneler.metin: So how do you put this to use? Here are five practical tips.
One. Treat frozen as a reliable default, not a compromise. If fresh vegetables would sit in your fridge for more than a few days, frozen may match or beat them for vitamin C.
sahneler.gorsel: an open freezer drawer with several bags of frosted broccoli florets, spinach and peas neatly stacked

sahneler.metin: Two. Buy fresh when it's truly fresh, from a farm stand or your own garden, and eat it within a day or two. Just-picked is when fresh is at its best.
sahneler.gorsel: a farm stand table with crates of freshly picked broccoli, carrots and green beans, a hand-lettered blank board hanging above

sahneler.metin: Three. Use fresh vegetables within a few days, and don't leave them waiting. The longer they sit, the more vitamin C they lose.
sahneler.gorsel: a refrigerator shelf with a head of broccoli at the front, a bag of spinach and a carton behind, a small pocket watch on the shelf

sahneler.metin: Four. Cook gently and briefly. Microwave or steam with a little water rather than boiling for a long time, and if you do boil, use the cooking water in a soup, since some of the vitamins end up there.
sahneler.gorsel: a steaming pot of vegetable soup with broccoli florets floating in it, a ladle resting on the rim, a small bowl of broccoli beside it

sahneler.metin: Five. Read the label. Plain frozen vegetables, without added sauce, butter or salt, keep the choice in your hands. And mix things up, because variety matters more than any single winner.
sahneler.gorsel: a plain bag of frozen broccoli florets beside a bag of mixed frozen vegetables on a counter, a bowl of broccoli in front

sahneler.metin: A short note. If a doctor or dietitian has given you specific advice about vegetables, for example because of a medical condition or a medicine, keep following it.
sahneler.gorsel: a consultation desk with a stethoscope, a closed notebook and a small bowl of steamed broccoli

sahneler.metin: Let's recap.

kart.alt: Fresh at harvest · frozen after days

sahneler.metin: In controlled comparisons, frozen vegetables had vitamin C and other vitamins at levels comparable to fresh ones kept in the fridge, and sometimes higher.
sahneler.gorsel: a bowl of frosted broccoli florets and a bowl of fresh broccoli florets side by side on a white cloth, equal in size

sahneler.metin: Fresh wins when it's truly fresh, just picked and eaten quickly. Frozen can win when fresh has travelled and waited. Beta-carotene is one nutrient where some frozen vegetables fell behind.
sahneler.gorsel: a head of broccoli with a few drops of dew on a garden bed on the left, a frosted bag of broccoli florets on a kitchen counter on the right

sahneler.metin: And how you cook matters. Short, gentle cooking, like microwaving, keeps more vitamin C than long boiling.
sahneler.gorsel: a glass dish of bright green steamed broccoli florets on a table, a thin curl of steam rising

sahneler.metin: The best vegetables are the ones you actually eat. Fresh or frozen, the goal is more vegetables on your plate.
sahneler.gorsel: a dinner plate with a generous portion of broccoli, carrots and green beans next to a piece of grilled fish, on a wooden table

sahneler.metin: If you found this useful, subscribe to The Food Almanac for more food science, explained calmly and honestly. This video is for education only, and it isn't medical advice. See you in the next one.
